newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Efforts to form Bosnian central bank test unity.
newsitem.headline: Efforts to form Bosnian central bank test unity.

text.p: Bosnia's fragile peace and efforts to reunify the divided country could stand or fall on efforts to form a central bank and a single currency, foreign experts said on Tuesday.

Recovering from a devastating 43-month war, Bosnia is going through a painful political process of creating joint institutions comprised of former enemies which signed a U.S-brokered peace accord in November 1995.

But plans to form a single central bank and currency have been delayed for months. Leaders of Bosnia's Serb entity are insisting on a separate currency and special arrangements which would undermine the bank's authority, said a spokesman for the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt.
"The central bank is the key test for the unity of Bosnia- Hercegovina and it's a vitally important part of the reintegration process," spokesman Colum Murphy said.
Bosnia's peacetime central government, which rules over Serb and Moslem-Croat territories, has been virtually paralysed because Serb officials remain opposed to a unified state.
Under the Dayton accords, the central bank is supposed to have Serb, Moslem and Croat board members with an IMF-appointed foreign governor who can cast tie-breaking votes.
"Unless the central bank is in place, Dayton (the 1995 peace agreement) goes down too," one economic expert said.
"The policy makers on the Serb side feel that if they agree to a central bank, they're caving in to the consolidated state," the expert, who asked not to be named, said.
Diplomats say the Dayton agreement clearly precludes anything but one central bank issuing a single currency for Bosnia's Moslem-Croat federation and Serb republic.
"It would be like each one of the twelve federal reserve banks in the U.S. deciding to become independent," the expert said.
The Serb stance has prevented the adoption of the proposed law on the central bank, which Western experts have been discussing with Serb officials for the last two months.
The draft law, drawn up by the International Monetary Fund, has to be presented to the national parliament for adoption before the bank begins to exercise its authority.

The newly-appointed bank governor Serge Robert dismissed concerns, telling Reuters agreeing to each article in the draft law was a slow process but said both sides supported the concept of one bank and one currency.
The currency name and design, the structure of branch offices and the division of foreign reserves were among the issues which he and IMF representatives were trying to resolve, Robert said.
One proposal would allow for bank notes to carry an indentical front but with different designs on the back of the notes for the Serb and Moslem-Croat entities.
However Robert said nothing had been decided yet on the currency design.
He dismissed concerns from the federation and foreign analysts that such a solution could effectively create two currencies circulating in different areas and damage the central bank's authority.
"There is no question to make one currency for one entity. The branches will not undermine our authority because they will be appointed by the governor," Robert said.
Saying that patience would win the day, he said the bank could be operational by June or even earlier. "I'm optimistic because I think that finally, we will reach an agreement."

Failure to adopt the central bank law and a package of reforms proposed by the IMF has forced the postponement of an international donors' conference devised to raise funds for economic reconstruction.
The conference has been pushed back to mid-April from March.
